cards.front: The early embryonic divisions that produce smaller cells without growth are called {{c1::cleavage}}.
cards.quote: After fertilization the egg divides without growing, a process called cleavage, into a ball of smaller cells.

cards.front: What structure defines an amphibian blastula?
cards.back: A sphere of cells surrounding a fluid-filled cavity.
cards.quote: In amphibians the ball becomes a blastula, a sphere of cells around a fluid-filled cavity.

cards.front: What major rearrangement of cells occurs during gastrulation?
cards.back: Cells move from the surface inward, and the embryo sorts into ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm.
cards.quote: Then comes gastrulation, the stage at which cells move from the surface to the inside and the embryo sorts itself into three germ layers:

cards.front: The germ layer that gives rise to both epidermis and the nervous system is the {{c1::ectoderm}}.
cards.quote: The ectoderm, the outer layer, makes the epidermis, the outer layer of the skin, and the nervous system.

cards.front: Which germ layer lines the gut and forms organs such as the liver?
cards.back: The endoderm, the inner germ layer.
cards.quote: The endoderm, the inner layer, lines the gut and forms organs such as the liver.

cards.front: Where is the dorsal lip in an amphibian gastrula?
cards.back: At the edge of the initial blastopore groove, on the future back of the embryo.
cards.quote: the edge of that groove is the dorsal lip, on what will become the back

cards.front: What happens to the neural plate as the neural tube forms?
cards.back: The strip of dorsal ectoderm rolls up into the neural tube.
cards.quote: The brain and spinal cord come from a strip of ectoderm along the back, the neural plate, which later rolls up into the neural tube.

cards.front: Suppose belly ectoderm were already irreversibly committed to skin. What would happen beside a dorsal-lip graft, and why would neural tissue there challenge that claim?
cards.back: It would remain skin if commitment were irreversible. Neural tissue would show that neighbouring tissue can redirect its fate; it would not prove that back and belly ectoderm started identical.
cards.quote: If belly ectoderm becomes neural beside a dorsal lip, it was not fixed as skin.

cards.front: In the newt dorsal-lip graft, why does tracing cell ancestry help distinguish induction from the graft simply growing into extra tissue?
cards.back: Host-derived neural tissue at a site that would normally become belly skin shows that neighbouring cells changed fate; donor-derived tissue alone could reflect development of the graft itself.
cards.quote: Natural colour became a lineage marker, a visible trait that shows which embryo a cell came from.
cards.section: The graft: whose cells built the second back?

cards.front: How did the interspecies newt dorsal-lip graft make donor and host contributions distinguishable?
cards.back: A pale donor dorsal lip was placed in a pigmented host’s flank or belly. Pigment in sections distinguished host cells from donor cells.
cards.quote: Cells of taeniatus carry pigment granules that stay visible after the embryo is fixed and cut into thin sections.
cards.section: The graft: whose cells built the second back?

cards.front: In the newt dorsal-lip graft, how do self-differentiation and induction differ?
cards.back: Self-differentiation is the graft developing according to its own origin. Induction is the graft changing the fate of neighbouring host tissue.
cards.quote: The graft's cells develop according to their own origin and supply the new neural tissue themselves
cards.section: The graft: whose cells built the second back?

cards.front: In a hypothetical pale-donor graft into a pigmented newt host, a second neural tube has 425 pigmented and 75 pale cells. Assuming a reliable marker, what percentage is induced host tissue?
cards.back: Total = 425 + 75 = 500 cells. Host share = 425/500 × 100 = 85%; donor share = 75/500 × 100 = 15%. Most of the tube is induced host tissue.
cards.quote: In one embryo, most of the second neural tube was pigmented, and so made of host cells
cards.section: The graft: whose cells built the second back?

cards.front: A pale newt dorsal-lip graft produces a pale notochord beneath an entirely pigmented second neural tube. Does host origin of the tube mean the graft itself failed to differentiate?
cards.back: No. The pale notochord shows donor self-differentiation, while the pigmented neural tube shows induction of host ectoderm. Both processes can occur in the same graft.
cards.quote: The graft's own cells self-differentiated into that notochord and mesoderm, so both happened at once.
cards.section: The graft: whose cells built the second back?

cards.front: A responding tissue’s ability to answer an inducing signal is called {{c1::competence}}.
cards.quote: The responder has to be able to answer it, and that ability is called competence.

cards.front: Why does failure to induce a tissue fate not, by itself, show that the inducer stopped signalling?
cards.back: The responder may have lost competence even if the inducer still sends a signal.
cards.quote: Without the inducer, or without competence, that induction does not happen

cards.front: Early-gastrula organizer is paired with amphibian ectoderm of increasing age. What happens to neural induction as gastrulation ends, and why?
cards.back: The neural response falls and largely stops. The ectoderm loses competence to answer the organizer’s signal as gastrulation ends.
cards.quote: The response falls with the age of the ectoderm: in amphibians, by the end of gastrulation it largely stops forming neural tissue in such tests.

cards.front: Late amphibian ectoderm fails to become neural beside organizer tissue. Which additional age combination can show that an older organizer still signals?
cards.back: Pair late organizer with early ectoderm. Neural tissue in that combination shows that the older organizer remains active and supports loss of competence in the older responder.
cards.quote: The extra combination is late organizer wrapped in early ectoderm.

cards.front: In a new tissue system, an old signalling tissue paired with an old responder no longer changes fate. Design comparisons that distinguish failure of the source from loss of responder competence.
cards.back: Pair the old source with a known competent young responder, and the old responder with a known active young source; include a young–young positive control. Induction needs both an active source and a competent responder, so the crossed pairings test the two possible failures separately.
cards.quote: If that still gives neural tissue, the organizer is still signalling, and the loss is in the responder.

cards.front: A signalling region that coordinates neighbouring tissues into an ordered body axis is an {{c1::organizer}}.
cards.quote: An organizer is a signalling region that can make its neighbours form a coordinated set of tissues, here a whole axis, in the right order.
cards.section: More than one induction: the organizer builds an axis

cards.front: What three contributions account for the coordinated second axis in the newt organizer graft?
cards.back: Donor cells form notochord and dorsal mesoderm; recruited host mesoderm takes dorsal fates; induced host ectoderm forms neural tissue.
cards.quote: The organizer's own cells became notochord and other dorsal mesoderm (pale in the sections). It recruited neighbouring host mesoderm into dorsal fates such as somites.
cards.section: More than one induction: the organizer builds an axis

cards.front: What are somites in the amphibian second axis?
cards.back: Blocks of mesoderm beside the neural tube that form vertebrae and muscle.
cards.quote: somites, blocks of mesoderm beside the neural tube that form vertebrae and muscle
cards.section: More than one induction: the organizer builds an axis

cards.front: How does an instructive signal differ from a permissive signal?
cards.back: An instructive signal chooses an outcome; a permissive signal allows an outcome chosen by something else.
cards.quote: A permissive signal allows an outcome that something else chooses; an instructive signal chooses the outcome itself.
cards.section: More than one induction: the organizer builds an axis

cards.front: A signal is hypothesized to permit neural tissue only at a host’s preselected back. Its source is moved beside competent belly ectoderm. What pattern does that hypothesis predict, and why?
cards.back: Neural tissue should remain at the preselected back, with belly ectoderm remaining skin. Under that hypothesis, another host feature chooses the location; the signal only permits it.
cards.quote: If the organizer only allowed neural tissue where the host had already marked out a back, where should neural tissue form?
cards.section: More than one induction: the organizer builds an axis

cards.front: Why does a neural plate following a moved signal source not prove that the signal directly activates neural fate?
cards.back: Removing a local brake could make the plate follow the source too. The experiment establishes instruction for place, but does not distinguish activation from disinhibition.
cards.quote: If it releases a brake, the neural fate itself was the ectoderm's own, and the organizer would be permissive for neural fate yet still instructive for place.
cards.section: More than one induction: the organizer builds an axis

cards.front: In a hypothetical system, a local signal specifies where a fate forms, but only competent cells respond. Its source moves within a competent field, then beyond it. Assuming only nearby cells receive the signal, what happens and why?
cards.back: The fate follows the source within the competent field but fails to appear outside it. This combines the move-the-source rule for position with the rule that induction requires competence. The second failure alone does not show that signalling stopped.
cards.quote: If the pattern follows the source, the signal is instructive for place: it decides where the pattern forms.
cards.section: More than one induction: the organizer builds an axis

cards.front: In Xenopus, β-catenin fails to stabilize on the future dorsal side after fertilization. What happens to activation of organizer genes, and why?
cards.back: The normal dorsal activation of organizer genes is disrupted. Stabilized dorsal β-catenin normally enters nuclei and, with signals from the yolky cells below, switches those genes on.
cards.quote: β-catenin, the Wnt pathway's transcriptional co-activator, is stabilized on the future dorsal side and enters nuclei there
cards.section: More than one induction: the organizer builds an axis

cards.front: What distinction did killed-newt-organizer assays reveal between neural induction and organizing a body axis?
cards.back: Killed organizer often made competent ectoderm neural, but did not build an organized second axis. Neural-inducing activity survived cell death; full organizing activity did not.
cards.quote: Organizing did not: killed tissue made ectoderm neural but did not build an organized second axis in these tests.

cards.front: What is the difference between a factor being sufficient and being necessary for an effect?
cards.back: Sufficient means it can produce the effect by itself under the tested conditions. Necessary means the effect does not occur without it.
cards.quote: A factor is sufficient if it is enough, by itself, to produce an effect. It is necessary if the effect does not happen without it.

cards.front: Why did neural induction by killed tissues and unrelated materials leave the natural organizer signal unidentified?
cards.back: Many materials scored positive. A positive neural assay could reflect the natural signal or an indirect release of neural tendency, so sufficiency did not identify the embryo’s signal.
cards.quote: When almost everything scores yes, a yes cannot name the signal.

cards.front: A candidate substance makes competent ectoderm neural. Design a further test of whether it is required during neural induction in an embryo.
cards.back: Remove or block the candidate during induction, with a matched untreated control; check that the responder remains competent. Test whether restoring the candidate restores induction. The stated necessity rule asks whether the effect fails without the candidate; the original addition assay tested only sufficiency.
cards.quote: But sufficient does not mean natural: a factor can be enough to produce an effect without being the signal the embryo uses.

cards.front: Some cultured Ambystoma ectoderm forms neural tissue without an organizer. Which claim about organizer necessity does this challenge, and how far does the result generalize?
cards.back: It challenges the claim that an organizer is always necessary for neural tissue. The conclusion applies to that ectoderm in those culture conditions, not automatically to all embryos.
cards.quote: for that ectoderm, an organizer was not even necessary for neural tissue to form.

cards.front: Suppose competent amphibian ectoderm has a neural tendency held back by a signal. What would a nonlethal injury that weakened that brake do, and why?
cards.back: It could produce neural tissue without supplying the natural organizer signal. Weakening the brake would release the ectoderm’s existing neural tendency.
cards.quote: If neural is what ectoderm becomes when a brake is released, then many injuries and chemicals that weaken the brake would be expected to "induce" as well.

cards.front: Why does loss of competence for one inducing signal not mean a developing tissue has lost all ability to respond to signals?
cards.back: Competence is specific to a response. Amphibian ectoderm largely loses competence for organizer-driven neural induction after gastrulation but still responds to other signals later.
cards.quote: After that the ectoderm's competence for the organizer's neural induction has largely gone, though it still answers other signals later in development.

cards.front: Organizer and competent ectoderm are placed across a porous filter that passes molecules but blocks cells and their processes. What controls are needed before neural induction supports a diffusible signal?
cards.back: Use a solid sheet of the same thickness, and ectoderm on the filter without organizer. Induction across the filter, but not in either control, supports a diffusible signal being sufficient.
cards.quote: A solid sheet in place of the filter, and ectoderm on the filter with no organizer, are the controls.

cards.front: No neural tissue forms across a porous filter between organizer and ectoderm. Why is that insufficient to establish a contact requirement, and what comparisons would strengthen interpretation?
cards.back: Failure could reflect an inactive source or incompetent responder rather than lack of contact. Test the same tissues together as a positive control and verify that the filter passes molecules. This combines the competence rule with the filter assay; a negative result alone does not establish a contact requirement.
cards.quote: The pores should let molecules through but be too small for cells or their processes to cross.

cards.front: Killing one frog blastomere and leaving it attached produced partial embryos, while separating sea-urchin blastomeres produced small whole larvae. Why can these results alone not isolate intrinsic differences in cell fate?
cards.back: Species and treatment both differed, including whether a dead sister cell remained attached. The rule is to separate competing explanations before assigning cause. The later formation of whole embryos after complete frog-cell separation further weakens the claim that the frog result proved fixed half-embryo fates.
cards.quote: The experiments differed in species, and in one detail that mattered: Roux's dead cell stayed attached to its living sister.
cards.section: Roux, Driesch and the loop of hair

cards.front: After hair-loop separation of a newt embryo, one half remains alive and divides but has neither neural plate nor notochord. Does cell survival establish successful axis formation?
cards.back: No. The living “belly piece” shows that survival and division can occur without building an axis; those readouts must be distinguished from organized development.
cards.quote: Cells could live and divide without building an axis.
cards.section: Roux, Driesch and the loop of hair

cards.front: Why did the dorsal-lip graft alone not establish the classical claim that underlying mesoderm normally induces ectoderm?
cards.back: It showed that transplanted dorsal-lip tissue can induce. Demonstrating that underlying mesoderm is the normal source required later work.
cards.quote: The 1924 graft showed that dorsal-lip tissue can induce; it did not itself show that the mesoderm underneath is the normal source

cards.front: In a pale-donor, pigmented-host newt graft, some host descendants inherit too few pigment granules to be recognized. What happens to the estimated host contribution, and why?
cards.back: It is underestimated if this is the only error: pale-looking host cells are misclassified as donor. The net error remains unknown if donor cells can also be misclassified.
cards.quote: A host cell that inherits few granules can look pale and be counted as donor, which would understate the host's share.
cards.section: How far to trust a pigment marker

cards.front: A newt graft’s pigment counts may misclassify both host and donor cells. How would you strengthen the lineage inference, and why can you not simply correct the host fraction upward?
cards.back: Use an independent donor dye label and compare it with pigment assignments to assess errors in both directions. The pigment-marker rule says that unmeasured opposing errors have unknown net size and direction; the lineage-design section supplies the more reliable dye approach.
cards.quote: Without measuring how often each mistake happens, neither the size nor the direction of the net error is known.
cards.section: How far to trust a pigment marker
